A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SLAM system despite its renaming from Scaffold-SLAM to SEGS-SLAM. Their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. v2 ends with references; v3 additionally contains supplementary Sections 7–12, which were included in the comparison.

before.justification: v2 Section 4 reports original rendering-quality, camera-tracking, runtime and component-ablation results on Replica, TUM RGB-D and EuRoC.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark and ablation results in Section 5, with further controlled analyses and per-scene results in the supplement.

M1.justification: The stated frequency objective changes from a shared coefficient in v2 Equation 7 to scale-specific weights in v3 Equation 9. The principal pipeline remains ORB-SLAM3, voxelized anchor-based Gaussians, pose-conditioned AfME and multiscale frequency regularization. SEPM largely names and elaborates the structured initialization already described in v2 Section 3.2.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate monocular and RGB-D SLAM on Replica and TUM RGB-D, and stereo SLAM on EuRoC. v3 specifies the evaluated sequences and adds per-scene breakdowns, without establishing an expansion to new tasks, domains or camera conditions.

E2.justification: v3 adds SGS-SLAM to Replica RGB-D rendering/tracking comparisons and the runtime comparison. GO-SLAM and Photo-SLAM-30K disappear from the tracking tables, while GS-SLAM's rendering-speed entry is omitted from the relocated runtime table. The principal rendering comparator set otherwise remains.

E3.justification: New analyses introduce an original-3D-GS control for SEPM, a one-to-four-level frequency-pyramid sweep, low/high-frequency alternatives, and a fixed rendering viewpoint with varied AfME input poses. The retained benchmark protocols still exclude training views and RGB-D masks and use the same metric families. Newly disclosed settings do not establish that existing experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's AfME/FRP removal and replacement studies, v3 directly isolates SEPM, probes appearance control at a fixed viewpoint, tests pyramid depth and frequency components, and visualizes anchor densification (Table 4, Tables 5–6, Figures 5, 8 and 10). The replacement study is retained in supplementary Table 7, where the frequency replacement is explicitly defined as single-scale high-frequency regularization.

E5.justification: v3 Section 5.1 newly states that results are averaged across five runs. v2 provides no repeated-run count. This adds statistical reporting without establishing an increase in runs; neither version supplies confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Numerous benchmark and ablation values are revised, and v3 adds per-scene results in Tables 9–13. Ours' TUM monocular PSNR changes from 24.52 to 25.17, while GS-ICP's TUM RGB-D PSNR changes from 21.25 to 17.81. DROID-SLAM's stereo ATE changes from 38.590 to 1.926 cm while Ours remains 7.462 cm, changing the tracking leader. These are revised reported results, not established controlled performance gains across versions.

T1.justification: The frequency-loss definition gains scale-specific weighting in v3 Equation 9. v3 also documents explicit anchor-position, voxelization and refinement formulas, while omitting v2 Equation 9's explicit volume-loss definition. The bundle-adjustment and alpha-blending relations are substantially retained; no theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: v2 presents AfME and frequency regularization as its two principal innovations. v3 instead foregrounds SEPM and AfME, claiming the first SLAM framework to initialize anchors from ORB-SLAM3 point clouds. Frequency regularization remains but is described as a minor improvement. This substantially redefines the claimed contribution, while retaining superiority claims across the same camera modalities.

C2.justification: v3 develops structural preservation through fixed anchors as a central mechanism and interprets low-frequency supervision as conflicting with structured Gaussians. It replaces v2's MAP-distribution rationale for AfME with spatial-context and continuity arguments. New limitations identify dependence on well-structured point clouds, static-scene restrictions for AfME and rendering-speed costs (Sections 4.1–4.2, 5.4 and 8–9).

D1.justification: v3 adds extensive implementation information: thread organization, keyframe sampling, MLP architectures and activations, embedding dimensions, voxel sizes, ten Gaussians per anchor, refinement thresholds and intervals, pruning rules, and loss weights. It newly specifies a common 30K iteration cap and supplies a project-page link. These substantially expand documentation; the PDFs do not establish downloadable code availability or changes to previously unspecified settings.

R1.justification: Research positioning shifts toward the claimed novel structural combination of ORB-SLAM3 and Scaffold-GS. v3 adds references including SGS-SLAM, DG-SLAM, COLMAP and Neural Rerendering in the Wild, revises the appearance-embedding lineage, and removes the concurrent-work discussion including OG-Mapping and LoopSplat. These changes extend beyond bibliographic renumbering or publication updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and method narrative are substantially rewritten around structural preservation. v3 introduces a Preliminaries section, reorganizes component explanations and ablations, moves some bundle-adjustment details, runtime discussion and replacement studies into the supplement, and changes method terminology and the title.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the system overview, adds SEPM and appearance-embedding diagrams and network schematics, revises benchmark panels and ablation illustrations, and expands annotated qualitative comparisons. Runtime columns become a separate supplementary table, while new per-scene tables substantially expand the presentation of evidence.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens experimental attribution and reproducibility. Compared with v2, it directly isolates structured initialization, tests frequency-design choices, demonstrates controlled AfME behavior, and supplies detailed architectures and hyperparameters (Table 4, Tables 5–7, Figure 5 and Section 11). Explicit limitations and per-scene results further improve assessability. Unexplained score revisions and inconsistent tracking averages, including in v3 Table 11, remain weaknesses, but the added controls and technical disclosure address substantial gaps in v2.
